reason: There are over 14 distinct claims about the cloud's discovery, physical properties, and 'jiggling' behavior that are supported by multiple sources.
story: Floating in the constellation Ophiuchus is a terrifying ink-black void known as Barnard 68. At first glance, it looks like a literal hole in the universe where stars have been erased. Discovered in 1919, this molecular cloud is so dense and close to Earth—about 400 light-years away—that not a single star can be seen through it or even in front of it. It is a half-light-year-wide ball of freezing cosmic dust with temperatures dropping to nearly absolute zero. But this 'empty' void is a lie. Using infrared telescopes, astronomers found thousands of stars hiding behind its curtain. Even stranger, the cloud isn't static; it is vibrating and 'jiggling' like a giant soap bubble or a water-filled balloon. This cosmic quivering is a prelude to collapse. Within 200,000 years, gravity will finally win, the void will implode, and this terrifying dark spot will ignite into a brand-new star.
angle: Barnard 68 is so dense and close to Earth that it creates a perfectly black 'hole' where no stars can be seen, yet the entire cloud is 'jiggling' like a giant soap bubble.

claims.claim: Barnard 68 is located in the southern constellation of Ophiuchus.
The cloud is approximately 407 light-years away from Earth.
American astronomer Edward Emerson Barnard added the nebula to his catalog in 1919.
Barnard 68 is classified as a Bok globule and a dark absorption nebula.
It is so opaque that background stars cannot be seen through it at visible-light wavelengths.
The cloud measures approximately half a light-year across.
Its temperature is extremely cold, estimated between 10 and 16 Kelvin.
The mass of the cloud is approximately twice that of the Sun.
The cloud is oscillating or vibrating in a manner similar to a jiggling soap bubble or water balloon.
It is expected to collapse and form a star within the next 200,000 years.
Infrared observations by the Very Large Telescope revealed roughly 3,700 background stars hidden behind the cloud.
Barnard 68 is frequently confused with the Boötes Void in media and articles.
There are no foreground stars between Earth and the cloud, making its blackness appear uninterrupted.
The cloud consists of gas and dust, including molecules that contain carbon.

disputed: Distance: S1, S3, and S4 cite 407 light-years, S2 cites 500, and S5 cites 300-400; the script should use 'about 400 light-years'.
Temperature: S1 and S3 cite 16 Kelvin while S2 and S5 cite 10 Kelvin; the script should attribute this to 'extreme cold near absolute zero'.
Mass: S1, S3, and S4 cite twice the mass of the Sun, while S5 says it is 'roughly the same mass' as the Sun; the script should say 'up to twice the mass'.
